To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the active site residues of UDG contribute to the interaction with the inhibitor protein, Ugi, but not to the same extent as to catalysis.
The mutational analyses of the active site residues, D64 and H 187, in Escherichia col UDG, revealed that they contribute significantly to the catalysis, but minimally to the binding with Ugi.
The active site residues of UDG, D64 and H 187, are crucial to its catalytic activity but contribute minimally to its interaction with Ugi, an inhibitor protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the structural and mechanistic basis of UDG catalysis and its interaction with Ugi, which will help us in designing inhibitors for the enzyme.
the molecular mechanism of the UDG-Ugi interaction, which is crucial for the understanding of the regulation of base excision repair.
the molecular mechanism of UDG and Ugi, and how the two proteins interact with each other.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the catalytic residues are essential for catalysis, and that the residues that are essential for catalytic activity are minimally required in the interaction with the inhibitor protein.
D64 and the H187 are the catalytic residues of E. coli UDG, which are essential for catalysis but not for the interaction with Ugi.
D64 and to a lesser extent H187 are important for the catalysis of uracil excison by UDG, but not for the interaction of UDG with Ugi.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the catalytic residues of the UDGs have been identified and characterized in the past, but the role of these residues in the protein-protein interaction is still not well understood.
D64 and His187 are essential for catalysis, and that the Ugi-UDG interaction is independent of these residues.
UDGs are highly efficient in excising uracil from DNA and the active site residues are essential for this function, but are not critical to the interaction of UDG with Ugi.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the active site residues of UDGs are not essential for the interaction with Ugi and that the interaction between the proteins can be studied in the absence of these residues.

the active site residues, D64 and H185, of E. coli UDG, contribute minimally to its interaction with the inhibitor protein Ugi, and thus, the interaction between these two proteins is not driven by a simple lock-and-key mechanism.
the active site residues of UDG can be classified into two groups: those that contribute to the interaction with Ugi and those that contribute to catalysis.
